title: Musonius on marriage
hook: Musonius called marriage a full partnership of care (Musonius Rufus, Lecture 13)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Scipio's dream, Rome a tiny point from the stars, fame short, service still worth doing. Your line was from the stars. Did you rise for a breath when you wanted credit? Day six hundred forty-eight.

Who handles the dentist appointments in your house? Who remembers birthdays, notices the milk is low, sits up with the sick kid? Couples argue about it, and the question is old. In the Roman world, marriage was usually arranged around property, heirs and family alliances, and the law gave husbands far more room than wives. Then a Stoic teacher in Rome, the man who taught Epictetus, gave a lecture describing marriage in terms that still sound fresh. Today: koinōnia.
screen: `WHO REMEMBERS THE BIRTHDAYS?` → `ROMAN MARRIAGE: PROPERTY AND HEIRS.` → `EPICTETUS'S TEACHER SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher. Gaius Musonius Rufus taught Stoicism in Rome in the first century AD, and was exiled more than once by emperors who didn't like him. He wrote nothing we have. His lectures survive because a student wrote them down and a later anthologist, Stobaeus, kept them. Second, the lecture. Asked what the chief purpose of marriage is, Musonius answers: a shared life, and children. But children alone aren't enough, he says; animals have offspring too. What makes a marriage is companionship and care for each other, in health and in sickness, at every moment. Each should want to outdo the other in caring. When that's present, he says, the marriage is beautiful. When each looks only to their own interest, it falls apart, even if they live under the same roof. Third, the surprising part for his time. In other lectures, Musonius argued that women should study philosophy, because they have the same reason and the same virtues as men, and that daughters should be educated like sons. He also held husbands to the same standard of faithfulness he expected of wives. He wasn't modern in everything: he still assigned men and women different work. But the center of his picture was a partnership. Fourth, what we can take, partnered or not. Musonius's test works for any close bond, a marriage, a friendship, a sibling: does each of you look to the other's good, or only your own?
screen: `THE TEACHER OF EPICTETUS.` · `A SHARED LIFE, CARE IN SICKNESS.` · `THE SAME STANDARD FOR BOTH.` · `WHOSE GOOD ARE YOU LOOKING TO?` · then, large: `FULL PARTNERSHIP.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind your closest bond: a partner, a friend, a sister, a parent. See their face. Now ask Musonius's question honestly: lately, have I been looking to their good, or mostly my own? No guilt, just a look. Then think of one small way to care for them this week that they wouldn't expect. Something from their list, not yours. The errand they dread. The call they'd love. Hold that one thing in mind. The bell holds the time.
Koinōnia. Musonius's word for marriage: a partnership of shared life and care, each trying to outdo the other. Today's word.
Your line: full partnership. Do your one unexpected act of care today, for a partner or a friend, and don't mention it. Day six hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Readers of Musonius Rufus often point to his Lecture 13 as an ancient description of marriage as mutual care and partnership.

original.note: Greek: partnership, sharing, communion. Musonius describes marriage as a koinōnia of life.

trapdoor: what you thought: ancient philosophers saw marriage only as property and heirs.
what it means: Musonius called marriage a full partnership of care, each outdoing the other in looking after them.
what a scholar hears: Musonius's lectures survive in Stobaeus via a student's notes; Lectures 3, 4, 12 and 13A together make him unusual among ancient writers on women and marriage.

notes: Musonius Rufus c. AD 30–100; exiled under Nero (to Gyara) and again under Vespasian. Confirm 'more than once'.
Lectures preserved in Stobaeus, from notes by a student (named Lucius in the tradition). Confirm.
Lecture 13A: companionship and care in health and sickness; each competing to outdo the other in care; marriage ruined when each looks to self. Paraphrased; confirm.
Lecture 3 (women should study philosophy), Lecture 4 (daughters educated like sons), Lecture 12 (same sexual standard for husbands). Confirm numbering (Lutz's numbering).
Roman marriage legal framing is simplified; confirm 'the law gave husbands far more room than wives' is fair.
Editor review (year 2): cut the unsourced 'couples argue about this more than almost anything' and 'which many Romans didn't', and the superlative 'one of the ancient world's clearest' in howItsDone.
